The oldest thing you will ever see is free and available every clear night. Step outside after dark and look up: that faint smudge in Andromeda is two and a half million years old. Its light began its journey before humans existed, before even our earliest ancestors walked upright. It crossed an ocean of emptiness, undeterred, and ended its travels in the back of your eye.

Starlight is a kind of correspondence from the past. Every photon is a small letter postmarked centuries ago, reporting on what a star was doing when it wrote the message. Some stars we can see are already dead—their light outlives them, the way a voice echoes in a canyon after the speaker has gone.

Astronomers call this "lookback time," the way telescopes function as time machines. Point an instrument at a distant quasar and you see the universe as it was billions of years ago—younger, hotter, stranger. We tend to imagine the night sky as a ceiling, a dome fixed overhead, but it's more like a depth than a height. The farther the object, the deeper into time you're looking. The stars aren't so much above us as behind us, embedded in the past like fossils in stone.

There's something both humbling and comforting in this. The universe keeps a record of itself, and it shares that record generously, broadcasting in every direction all at once.

So when you look up tonight, you aren't seeing the universe. You're seeing its memory—and for a moment, you get to hold it.
